title: Logging Strategies
description: Learn how to design and maintain effective logging strategies for production systems using Linux and Git-centric workflows.

data.text: Logging is the persistent memory of your production system. Without structured logs, incidents become mysteries, and mysteries become multi-hour outages. In this lesson, you will learn how to design a logging strategy that gives you enough detail to debug problems without drowning in noise.

We will focus on Linux-native tools such as `journald`, `rsyslog`, and log rotation with `logrotate`, while keeping a Git-friendly mindset: logs should be inspectable, reproducible, and safe to share with teammates.

Unstructured logs are plain text blobs that humans read but machines struggle to parse. Structured logs use a consistent format such as JSON, making them searchable and machine-readable. For production systems, structured logging is strongly recommended.

data.title: Watch Out
data.text: Never log secrets, passwords, API keys, or personally identifiable information (PII). Scrub sensitive fields before writing logs and review log retention policies regularly.
Modern Linux distributions use `systemd-journald` for journal logs, `rsyslog` or `syslog-ng` for forwarding and filtering, and `logrotate` for managing file size and retention.

items: journald: stores logs in binary journal files, accessible via `journalctl`
rsyslog: routes logs to files, remote servers, or databases
logrotate: rotates and compresses old logs based on size or time

data.title: Viewing recent error logs with journalctl
data.code:
journalctl -u payment-api --since today -p err

# Follow logs in real time
journalctl -u payment-api -f

data.text: Log Levels and When to Use Them

rows: Failures that affect a single request
Out of memory, port already in use

data.title: Pro Tip
data.text: Use INFO for healthy milestones, WARN for trends that may become problems, and ERROR for things that actually failed. Avoid logging everything at ERROR level because it trains teams to ignore real problems.

When you run multiple servers, logs should flow to a single searchable store. ELK Stack, Grafana Loki, and Datadog are common choices. The Git parallel is simple: just as you `git log` across branches, you query across servers.

items: Define a standard log format for all services
Enforce log rotation with a maximum size and retention period
Send logs to a centralized store in production
Set up alerts for ERROR and FATAL log spikes
Review logs weekly for recurring warnings

data.title: Summary
data.text: Logging strategies turn chaotic text into actionable signals. Use structured formats, set appropriate log levels, rotate logs automatically, and centralize them for searchability. Good logging cuts incident response time from hours to minutes.
